residency.test: Residence is determined by significant residential ties - a home, spouse and dependants in Canada - rather than a day count alone.
residency.deemed_resident: 183 days or more of presence makes you a deemed resident if you have no residential ties.
residency.worldwide_income: Yes for residents. Non-residents are taxed on Canadian-source income only.
residency.departure: Leaving Canada triggers a deemed disposition of most property at fair market value (the departure tax).

headline.provincial: added on top and varies widely - Alberta is lowest, Quebec highest
headline.capital_gains: 50% of gains are included in income
headline.note: the lowest federal rate was cut from 15% to 14% part-way through 2025, giving a blended 14.5% for the year

credits.name: Basic personal amount (federal)
credits.note: 16,129 basic amount at the 14.5% credit rate; reduced for income above roughly 177,882

credits.name: Canada employment amount
credits.note: 1,471 at the lowest rate, for employees only

employee.name: CPP base contribution
employee.note: on pensionable earnings between 3,500 and the 71,300 maximum

employee.name: Employment Insurance
employee.note: Quebec has a lower EI rate and its own parental insurance plan

ON.name: Ontario
ON.note: Ontario also levies a surtax on provincial tax above certain thresholds, and a health premium

QC.name: Quebec
QC.note: Quebec collects its own income tax on a separate return; federal tax is abated by 16.5% for Quebec residents, which this model does not apply

capital_gains.inclusion_rate: 50% of the gain is included in taxable income
capital_gains.principal_residence: exempt under the principal residence exemption for years designated as such
capital_gains.note: a proposed increase of the inclusion rate to 66.7% above 250,000 was announced and subsequently abandoned; confirm the current position before relying on it

quirks: Provincial tax is a genuinely large part of the bill - the same income can differ by more than ten points of effective rate between Alberta and Quebec.
Quebec residents file two returns: a federal T1 and a provincial TP-1 with Revenu Québec.
RRSP contributions are deducted from income and the deadline is 60 days after year end, so a contribution made in the first days of March still reduces the previous year's tax.
TFSA income is completely untaxed but the annual room is limited, and over-contributions are penalised at 1% per month.
Leaving Canada triggers a deemed disposition of most assets. Plan the departure date deliberately rather than discovering it afterwards.

reporting.authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA); Revenu Québec for Quebec residents
reporting.who_must_file: Anyone with tax payable, anyone disposing of capital property, and anyone wanting benefits such as the GST/HST credit or Canada Child Benefit - which require a return even with no income.

deadlines.what: T1 filing and payment deadline for 2025
Filing deadline if you or your spouse are self-employed
deadlines.note: any balance owing is still due 30 April

deadlines.what: RRSP contribution deadline for the 2025 tax year

forms.name: Pension, retirement, annuity and other income
Statement of business or professional activities
Foreign income verification statement (foreign property over 100,000)

documents_to_collect: All T4, T4A, T5 and T3 slips (most are also visible in CRA My Account)
Medical expense and charitable donation receipts
Records of foreign property if the cost exceeded 100,000 at any time - T1135 is separately penalised
Notice of assessment from last year, which shows RRSP room

penalties.late_filing: 5% of the balance owing plus 1% per full month, up to 12 months
penalties.repeat_late_filing: 10% plus 2% per month, up to 20 months
penalties.late_payment: interest at the prescribed rate, compounded daily
penalties.t1135: 25 per day, minimum 100 and maximum 2,500, even with no tax owing

sources.name: CRA - Federal and provincial tax rates

warnings: Provincial credits, surtaxes (Ontario) and health premiums are not modelled; only the provincial rate schedule is applied.
The Quebec federal abatement of 16.5% is not applied, so Quebec results overstate federal tax.
Provincial basic personal amounts are omitted, which overstates provincial tax at low incomes.
